findings.title: Google Calendar stores the zod SafeParse wrapper object as the credential key
findings.body: In refreshAccessToken, `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` returns a zod SafeParseReturnType ({ success, data }), and that whole object is then written to the DB via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. Previously the code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the parsed token). After this change the credential key becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}` instead of the token payload, so the next time the credential is loaded `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` fails and the Google Calendar integration breaks for every user whose token is refreshed. The fix is to use `key.data` (after checking success) as the value stored.

findings.title: Salesforce CalendarService uses prisma without importing it
findings.body: The newly added block in getClient calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)` but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma";` (check the import list — only jsforce, rrule, zod, calcom libs, types, getAppKeysFromSlug and parseRefreshTokenResponse are imported). This will fail TypeScript compilation / throw a ReferenceError at runtime whenever the Salesforce calendar service is instantiated.

findings.title: zoho-bigin passes the credential ID as the user ID to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens' third parameter is `userId`, and when credential sync is enabled it is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. zoho-bigin passes `credentialId` (the Credential row id) instead of a user id — unlike every other app in this PR which passes `credential.userId`. With syncing enabled, the self-hoster's sync endpoint receives a credential id where it expects a Cal.com user id, so token refreshes for zoho-bigin will look up the wrong user (or fail) and return tokens for the wrong account.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !== on a raw header value
findings.body: The endpoint authenticates by comparing `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` with a plain string inequality. This is a timing-attackable comparison on a secret that guards writing arbitrary OAuth credentials for any userId. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers).

findings.title: Salesforce token is refreshed on every client construction regardless of expiry
findings.body: getClient now performs a blocking refresh_token grant against login.salesforce.com and a DB write every time a SalesforceCalendarService is constructed — previously jsforce handled refreshing lazily only when needed. Every calendar operation (create/update/delete, and availability flows that construct services) now incurs an extra Salesforce auth round-trip plus a credential write, slowing requests and burning through Salesforce's refresh-token rotation / rate limits unnecessarily. It should check the stored token's expiry first and only refresh when needed.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token" and persisted
findings.body: When the parsed response has no refresh_token, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers (e.g. zoom, which merges parsedToken.data over the stored key) then write this placeholder into the credential in the DB, destroying the real refresh token and permanently breaking subsequent refreshes for that credential. If the provider omits a refresh token, the existing stored one should be preserved instead of a sentinel string.
